title: AWS: a small cloud, with clear boundaries
summary: One upload through the live V2 AWS system: what each service owns, how work moves, and where limits remain.
opening_answer: The browser reaches our application through CloudFront and an HTTP API. Separate Media and Processing Lambda applications own their data, queues and Aurora cluster. Video bytes go straight to private S3. Clips of 60 s or less encode in a Lambda; longer ones on finite Fargate workers that a bounded launcher starts on demand.

sections.title: Start with the shape of the system

blocks.text: **Media** owns people, assets, upload reservations, source ownership and playback grants. **Processing** owns jobs, attempts, retries, cancellation and worker leases.

CloudFront serves the frontend from private S3 and forwards `/api/*` to an HTTP API with Media and Processing routes. A Media Lambda authorizer validates the login cookie; each service checks the actor against its own records.

layers.label: CloudFront
layers.detail: Static files from private S3; API requests pass uncached.

layers.label: HTTP API
layers.detail: Invokes the matching domain Lambda. Login and health are public.

layers.label: Domain Lambda
layers.detail: Checks ownership; writes only its own database.

sections.title: Follow the bytes separately from the requests

blocks.text: Media reserves an owner-scoped S3 key and returns a short-lived presigned POST; the browser sends the file to private S3, bypassing API Gateway and Lambda bodies; Media checks the object and adopts its version as the source.
A client-supplied key proves neither ownership nor unchanged bytes. A worker reads the accepted version and writes job outputs, but cannot change the source, read Media's database or list objects.

blocks.title: Private is not network-private
blocks.text: Access is by bucket policy and IAM; a signed URL reaches S3's public endpoint for a limited time.

sections.title: Two databases, one Aurora cluster per service

blocks.text: Each service owns a database on **its own** Aurora Serverless v2 cluster (AD-29, #94), with separate credentials and schema history. Services exchange versioned messages, never cross-domain SQL.

spec.title: Before and after the database split (21 Oct)
rows: Shared: one can wake or stall both
spec.caption: Cleanup dropped each cluster's copy of the peer's database. Per-run stacks keep flags off (AD-22).

blocks.text: Rehearsed on a throwaway stack (`database-split-rehearsal.json`); pre-split snapshot kept; CD run 39644028238 green; Processing idle during the split.

Pause is point-in-time: 0.0 ACU at 18:07 UTC on 19 October, about 56 minutes after the last upload (after #273, on `daee44b`, pre-split); not proof of monthly cost, and scheduled rescans can briefly wake SQL. Databases sit in private subnets across two AZs, reached over TLS through narrow security groups; connections are per invocation, since an open one stops Aurora pausing.

sections.title: Messages coordinate work; SQL remains the record

blocks.text: Three SQS queues carry Processing commands, Processing work and Media results, each with a dead-letter queue. Messages hold identifiers and versioned facts, never video, secrets or presigned fields.

Outbox: commit the change and message intent in one SQL transaction; a publisher sends later; the receiver deduplicates. SQL plus SQS is not one transaction, so duplicates are expected and repair matters. EventBridge is a hint, not the owner of job state.

steps.detail: A small work message; the queue never stores video.

steps.label: RunTask

sections.title: Why Lambda coordinates and Fargate encodes

blocks.text: Lambda: short event-driven work (APIs, handlers, repair, launcher). Fargate: the FFmpeg pipeline with more CPU and memory, then stop.

blocks.text: The launcher counts running, stopping and unresolved launches against a cap of three, reserving before calling ECS and resolving ambiguous replies by task identity or same-token replay. Tasks have finite lifetime and deadline.

sections.title: Subnet choices and the egress tradeoff

blocks.title: The physical architecture, on one map
blocks.alt: Persistent V2-live physical topology: browser and Publisher through CloudFront and HTTP API; owner Lambda functions and one Aurora cluster per service in private subnets; a short-encode Lambda for clips of 60 s or less; finite Fargate encoders in public subnets; S3 and SQS outside the VPC. Direct video traffic is separate from API control traffic.
blocks.caption: Green: media bytes. Purple: SQL. Dark: requests and messages. Scroll sideways on a phone or open the full SVG.

blocks.text: Lambda and Aurora: private dual-stack subnets across two AZs. No NAT Gateway, paid interface endpoint, EC2 host, load balancer or Redis. Lambda reaches SQS, Parameter Store and ECS over IPv6 egress-only routes, plus an S3 gateway endpoint (also for image layers).

Fargate and migration tasks use public subnets with a temporary public IPv4; security groups allow their database connection and the database stays private. This avoids a NAT Gateway but gives those tasks public egress.
Dual-stack is a cost choice. The template defines the routes; the live smoke shows upload-to-playback works, not every route.

ECR holds versioned images, deployed by immutable digest. The worker role reads sources and writes outputs, with no Media database access; ECS injects its Processing SQL credential through the separate execution role.
Secrets are exact Parameter Store SecureString references, read per function over TLS. GitHub Actions gets short-lived AWS credentials via OpenID Connect, no stored key (not the site's user login).

CloudWatch alarms watch failure and backlog signals; EventBridge schedules repair and launch. A monthly Budget alerts via SNS but is no spend ceiling. 13 of 13 alarms OK at 14:57 UTC on 19 October (earlier source): not proof of coverage. Live V2 is persistent, launcher on by default; not the V1 per-session workflow.

sections.title: What the live measurements teach us

blocks.text: **19 October, three clips.** Fargate scaled 0 to 3 to 0, but about 37 s passed from queued work to first processing (about 25 s task startup), missing the 20 s target. The launcher woke within about 1 s. No source SHA recorded (`dc2-live-worker:1`, pre-#272/#273): historical.
**Nine-clip backlog.** 239 s, 2.26 jobs per minute, peak three workers, one fixed-cap run: no capacity guarantee. 18 sends for nine jobs; `daee44b` recheck: 9 of 9 done, empty queue, no purge.

blocks.title: Short lane vs Fargate (sl1021, 5 jobs per arm)

blocks.text: 35 to 80 s per job outside queue and encode is unexplained: 20 s end-to-end still missed. Five jobs per arm is small.

blocks.q: Why did processing take about 37 seconds to start?
blocks.a: About 25 s was Fargate startup; the rest queueing and launch. A warm pool would cut it but adds idle cost; short clips now use the Lambda lane.

blocks.q: Is a separate Aurora cluster per service deployed?
blocks.a: Yes. Since 21 October: Media keeps the original cluster, Processing a copy-on-write clone (AD-29, #94), applied by CD run 39644028238; both pause at 0 ACU.

blocks.q: Does the object stay private if the browser has a signed URL?
blocks.a: Yes; the signed URL is temporary delegated access to S3's endpoint.

blocks.q: Why keep SQL if there is a queue?
blocks.a: SQL holds authoritative jobs, leases and message records; SQS only transports and may redeliver.

blocks.q: Why not encode everything in Lambda?
blocks.a: Lambda caps at 900 s and 2 GB /tmp, so only clips of 60 s, 64 MiB and 1080p or less use it (#93).

blocks.q: What does the monthly budget guarantee?
blocks.a: Alerts at thresholds; it does not stop spending.

takeaways: Media and Processing own separate applications, credentials, releases and Aurora clusters (AD-29).
Uploads go direct to private S3; SQS carries metadata; SQL is the durable record.
Lambda handles APIs and clips of 60 s or less; a launcher starts finite Fargate encoders, cap three.
Aurora placement, subnets, IAM and S3 policy are distinct security boundaries.
0-to-3-to-0 scaling; 37 s Fargate queue wait vs 0.26 s on the Lambda lane; 20 s end-to-end still missed.
